study_identification_part.si4_title: Neuroanatomical heterogeneity and homogeneity in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To quantify neuroanatomical heterogeneity in structural MRI measures (cortical surface area, cortical thickness, subcortical volume, and intracranial volume) in individuals at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis (CHR-P) compared with healthy controls, and to assess whether neuroanatomical heterogeneity differs between CHR-P individuals who subsequently transitioned to psychosis and those who did not.
study_characteristics_part.sc3_study_design_other: Cross-sectional neuroimaging analysis with longitudinal clinical follow-up data. The study analyzed baseline structural MRI data and examined associations with subsequent transition to psychosis. Follow-up duration ranged from 1 to 194 months (mean = 28.07, SD = 32.50, median = 18.00 months). Transition rate was 14.31% (n=226/1579).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis:
Answer: One-tailed Welch's t-tests for group-level PBSI comparisons between CHR-P and HC; multivariable regression models (adjusting for age and sex) to examine moderating effects of transition status (CHR-T/CHR-NT), subgroup status (APS/BLIPS/GRD), antipsychotic exposure, and baseline psychopathology (CAARMS/SIPS severity z-scores) on PBSI scores; Variability Ratio (VR) and Coefficient of Variation (CV) analyses with False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons; leave-one-site-out resampling for sensitivity analyses. Within-group PBSI showed lower similarity in CHR-P vs HC for SA (t(2642)=-5.39, p<0.01), CT (t(2788)=-9.11, p<0.01), SV (t(2733)=-4.34, p<0.01). No significant associations between PBSI scores and transition to psychosis, subgroup status, or baseline psychopathology. A nominal association between typical antipsychotic use and PBSI-SV-Z (b=-0.84, t(1220)=-2.191, p=0.03) was found but not robust across other phenotypes.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed:
Answer: The study found no significant regional heterogeneity after FDR correction using Variability Ratio analyses, though trends were observed in frontal, temporal, and hippocampal regions (VR=1.06-1.08, representing 6-8% greater variability). However, Person-Based Similarity Index (PBSI) analyses revealed significantly greater within-group variability in CHR-P compared to HC across all neuroanatomical profiles: PBSI-SA (t(2642)=-5.39, p<0.01), PBSI-CT (t(2788)=-9.11, p<0.01), and PBSI-SV (t(2733)=-4.34, p<0.01). Normative PBSI analysis identified 11 CHR-P individuals (0.70%) with marked deviation (>1.5 SD) in surface area, 118 (7.47%) in cortical thickness, and 161 (10.20%) in subcortical volume. Only 17 participants showed marked deviation in more than one phenotypic profile, and just 1 participant in all three. Importantly, no significant associations were found between any measure of heterogeneity (VR, CV, or PBSI) and transition to psychosis, subgroup status (APS/BLIPS/GRD), or baseline psychopathology (CAARMS/SIPS severity). A nominal association between typical antipsychotic use and greater deviation in PBSI-SV-Z (b=-0.84, t(1220)=-2.191, p=0.03) was observed, but this was not robust across other neuroanatomical phenotypes. Follow-up duration ranged from 1-194 months (mean=28.07±32.50 months, median=18.00 months), with a transition rate of 14.31% (226/1579).
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative

caa10_key_limitations.answer:
Answer: Regional VR/CV indices produced conceptually discrepant findings from global PBSI scores - may reflect differences between group-level vs. individual-level approaches or regional vs. global patterns; small effect sizes (VR=1.06-1.08) that did not survive FDR correction for regional analyses; substantial variation in follow-up duration between sites, with potential misclassification of 'no transition' cases who may have developed psychosis after final data contribution; limited clinical variables available for characterizing the approximately 10% of individuals with marked PBSI deviations; only 13.68% of CHR-P sample on atypical antipsychotics and 0.95% on typical antipsychotics at baseline; 243 participants (15.4%) had neither CAARMS nor SIPS assessment scores; two sites excluded due to IRB restrictions, leading to smaller sample than original ENIGMA CHR-P study; inability to control for factors like substance use; need for longitudinal imaging data and external validation of heterogeneity indices.
Confidence Rating: High
Negative Answer Category: Not Negative
Reason: The discussion section explicitly addresses multiple limitations of the study, including methodological considerations (discrepancy between VR and PBSI, small effect sizes), data limitations (variable follow-up duration, missing clinical variables), sample characteristics (low antipsychotic use, missing assessments), and future research needs (longitudinal imaging, external validation).
Supporting Text: Discussion section addresses limitations including discrepancies between VR and PBSI findings, variable follow-up duration, limited clinical characterization data, need for longitudinal imaging and external validation

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study represents the largest analysis of neuroanatomical heterogeneity in CHR-P to date, using data from 29 international sites in the ENIGMA CHR-P consortium (N=2822 total participants). Key methodological strengths include comprehensive quality control following ENIGMA protocols (excluding participants with >5% missing ROIs), harmonization using neuroComBat to address multi-site scanner effects, and multiple sensitivity analyses (leave-one-site-out, age/sex/site-matched cohorts). FreeSurfer versions varied by site (5.1 to 6.0.0, detailed in eTable 2). The study introduces novel application of Person-Based Similarity Index (PBSI) to assess individual-level neuroanatomical deviation from normative profiles, complementing traditional group-level heterogeneity metrics (VR, CV). Importantly, the discrepancy between null findings for regional VR/CV and significant findings for global PBSI highlights the importance of analytical approach (regional group-level vs. global individual-level) in heterogeneity research. The study identified approximately 7-10% of CHR-P individuals with marked neuroanatomical deviation (>1.5 SD) in cortical thickness and subcortical volume, representing a potential subgroup for further clinical characterization and targeted intervention research. However, these deviations were not associated with transition to psychosis (follow-up: 1-194 months, mean 28.07±32.50, median 18.00; transition rate 14.31%). Future research directions include examining associations with other longitudinal outcomes (psychosocial functioning, non-psychotic psychopathology, symptom persistence), collecting longitudinal imaging data, and external validation of heterogeneity indices. Clinical high-risk assessments used CAARMS (Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States) or SIPS (Structured Interview for Psychosis-Risk Syndromes), with 243 participants (15.4%) having neither assessment. Antipsychotic use at baseline was relatively low (13.68% atypical, 0.95% typical). Study conducted according to RECORD Statement for observational studies using routinely-collected health data. Computer code for VR/CVR/PBSI calculations available from authors upon request. Full dataset details including site-specific MRI acquisition parameters provided in supplementary eTable 2 (lines 122-181 of 41398_2022_2057_MOESM1_ESM.docx.md).
